## Submission metadata

- **Conference:** Data Curation Conference 2027, Research Data Management Network, University of Basel, Thursday 14 January 2027
- **Format:** Workshop session, 75 minutes with discussion, 10:45 to 12:00, 10 to 20 participants
- **Presenter:** Lars Schöbitz
- **Discipline:** Global health engineering (water, sanitation and health)
- **Use case:** Survey and monitoring data from the water, sanitation and health sector, from the raw file to a published data package and website
- **Data curation aspect(s):** Presentation of data to humans, documentation, versioning, metadata, AI assisted curation with disclosure, sensitive data
- **Version:** Revised for the conference website on 10 November 2026 after the acceptance, with the agenda, the learning objectives and the prerequisites the organisers asked for. The version submitted on 21 October 2026 is release v1.0.0 of the repository https://github.com/Global-Health-Engineering/workshop-dcc-2027

## Abstract

Survey and monitoring data from the water, sanitation and health sector mostly lives in spreadsheets that only their owners can read. For five years, Global Health Engineering at ETH Zurich has turned such files into published data, for our own projects and, through openwashdata, for the wider sector. Versioned code processes the raw file into an analysis ready dataset with a data dictionary and machine readable metadata, packaged as an R data package, archived with a DOI, and presented on a website with documentation and plots built from the data. AI now does most of the mechanical work. We publish for machines and humans. This workshop is about the humans, who still have to discover, interpret and trust data that machines parse with ease.

The workshop starts before the conference. Participants send a dataset, their own or a published one under an open licence, and review the data package built from it, which is published with a website and a DOI before the day. In the workshop I run the workflow live, from a messy raw file to a data package and website, with the free, open source tool washr. Every step can be done by a person or by a coding agent. Here the agent performs them, and the points where a person confirms stay visible. pkgreview, the AI driven review that follows the build, is introduced. Participants then explore the published packages and each post one comment on what a human reader still misses, so every human and every AI intervention stays on the record. Everyone takes home a picture of what a published dataset looks like for a human reader, a worked example to judge the workflow for their own data, and a record of how AI took part. The discussion takes up, in groups, four themes the workflow raises for data curation: oversight of AI curation, disclosure of AI contributions, sensitive data, and scientific credit for data.

## Agenda (75 minutes)

The agenda is subject to change.

1. Introduction, 15 minutes. Why we publish for humans, the workflow in one picture, the three stages of data (raw, analysis ready, final), and the links to the participants' data packages.
2. Live run with washr, 20 minutes. From the raw file to a documented data package and its website. Every step (folder structure, data dictionary, metadata, README, website) can be done by a person or by a coding agent. The agent does them here, and the points where a person confirms are shown.
3. Review, release and DOI, 10 minutes. pkgreview introduced as the AI driven review. The steps after the build, with the disclosure trail (commit trailers, prompt archive), shown on a participant's package that has its DOI. Participants explore the published packages and each post one comment on the GitHub issue of one of them.
4. Discussion in groups, 25 minutes. Four groups, one theme each: oversight of AI curation, disclosure of AI contributions, sensitive data, scientific credit for data. Each group collects its points on sticky notes, and one person per group reports back.
5. Take home, 5 minutes. Where the packages and the guide are, how to try washr on your own data afterwards, who to ask.

## Learning objectives

After the workshop, participants can

- describe the stages a raw dataset passes through on its way to a published data package and website, and what a human reader needs at each stage (documentation, data dictionary, metadata, plots);
- tell which steps of data curation a coding agent can take over, which stay with the researcher, and how AI contributions are recorded so that they stay visible;
- judge from a worked example, their own package or another participant's, what it takes to publish their own data as a data package, and know where the tools and the guide are;
- weigh the four themes (oversight, disclosure, sensitive data, credit) for their own data and their own institution.

## Prerequisites

Three steps before the workshop, all by Friday 11 December 2026. The workshop website, https://rawtoweb.github.io/website/dcc-2027/, explains each of them.

- Step 1, required: take the ten minute pre-course survey. It records your GitHub username and walks you through creating an account if you have none.
- Step 2, required: post one comment on the check-in issue of the workshop repository. It tests your account. The website explains what an issue is.
- Step 3: send a dataset through the form on the workshop website, either your own data (a CSV or Excel file with a brief description) or a published dataset under CC BY 4.0 or CC0 that you pick. The data must hold no personal data. I build a data package from it, you review it, and it is published with a DOI before the conference, with you as an author. If you have no data to share, you say so in the survey.

Bring a laptop. No software has to be installed.
